CHANGES INCORPORATED Informational Report on Changes to Administrative Portions of University Manual, Chapters 1, 2, 4 , and 7 University Manual Part I Statutes and Rules for the Government of the University Chapter 1 The Board of Education, The Council on Postsecondary Education, and the President of the University Board of Education 1.10.10 Background.

On May 7, 1981, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that public higher education in Rhode Island should be regulated by a body called “Board of Governors for Higher Education.” In 2012, the Rhode Island General Assembly voted that, beginning with 2013, the Board of Governors should be replaced by a Board of Education, in charge of all of public education in Rhode Island.

9 1.10.11 Composition of the Board and Quorum Requirements.
The Board of Education is to consist of seventeen (17) public members appointed by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Rhode Island Senate.
The Chair of the Governor's Workforce Board, or designee, and the Chair of the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation, or designee, shall serve as non-­‐voting, ex-­‐officio members of the board.
The Governor shall select from the appointed members a chairperson and vice chairperson.
A quorum shall consist of nine (9) members of the board.
A majority vote of those present shall be required for action.
The Chair of the Board shall have no term and shall serve at the pleasure of the governor. 1.10.12 Chief Responsibility of the Board.
According to its webpage (http://www.ride.ri.gov/BoardofEducation/BoardMembers.aspx, accessed 1/5/17), “The Board of Education is the chief policy-­‐setting body overseeing K-­‐20 education in Rhode Island.
Through its designated powers and duties, the Board helps shape the course of public education to ensure that all of the state's students receive the best possible education.” Council on Postsecondary Education 1.20.10 Background.

In June of 2014, the Board of Education voted to establish two separate sub-­‐councils, one being the Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, the other being the Council on Postsecondary Education.
The Council on Postsecondary Education is chiefly in charge of those matters relating to the University of Rhode Island for which university-­‐internal approval is not sufficient. “The Council is an independent public corporation vested with the responsibility of providing oversight for the system of public higher education in Rhode Island.
This system consists of three public institutions of higher learning, the University of Rhode Island (URI), Rhode Island College (RIC), and the Community College of Rhode Island (CCRI), along with the Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner.
The Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner, which operates under the direction of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, is the administrative and research arm of the Rhode Island Council on Postsecondary Education.” (https://www.riopc.edu/page/Council%20overview/) 1.20.11 Composition of the Council.

The Council on Postsecondary Education comprises eight members appointed by the Governor from the members of the Board of Education, to serve until their terms on the Board expire, and one non-­‐voting student member appointed for a two-­‐year term from one of the three public Rhode Island institutions of higher learning.
The Council’s chair shall be appointed by the Governor from one of the eight voting members of the Council.
In addition, the Chair of the Board of Education shall serve on the Council in an ex officio, non-­‐voting capacity. (see RIGL §16-­‐59-­‐2). 1.20.12 Chief Responsibilities of the Council.
The Council’s responsibilities include (for more details, see Rhode Island General laws § 16-­‐59-­‐1 and § 16-­‐59-­‐4): (1) It shall retain all authority formerly vested in the Board of Education regarding the employment

10 of faculty and staff at the public higher education institutions. (2) It shall prepare and maintain a five (5) year funding plan for higher education that implements the strategic financing recommendations of the Board of Education. (3) It shall prepare with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education and to present annually to the State Budget Officer in accordance with § 35-­‐3-­‐4 a state higher education budget.

Prior to submitting the budget to the State Budget Officer as required by the budget office instructions and this subsection, the Council shall present the budget to the Board of Education for its review and approval. (4) It shall appoint and dismiss presidents of the public institutions of higher learning with the assistance of the Commissioner of Postsecondary Education, and to establish procedures for this, and with the assistance of the Commissioner to approve or disapprove vice presidents of the public institutions of higher learning appointed by the respective presidents of the public institutions of higher learning. (5) It shall delegate to the presidents of each public higher education institution the authority and responsibility for operational and management decisions related to their institutions, consistent with the goals of the statewide strategic plan for postsecondary education, provided however that the presidents may be required to provide information or updates to the council regarding any delegated operational or management decisions.
The President of the University 1.30.10 Presidential Powers—Shared Governance.

In 2014, the President of the University received authority over certain items that previously needed to be submitted for approval to the super-­‐ordinated state body (Board of Governors, Board of Regents, etc.).
The items over which the President now has authority include: “To create, and consolidate departments, divisions, programs, and courses of study within the university with the assistance of the commissioner of postsecondary education within the approved role and scope adopted by the council on postsecondary education pursuant to § 16-­‐59-­‐4” (See RI General Law § 16-­‐32-­‐2.1).

The law stipulates, however, that this authority is to be exercised “consistent with shared governance practices, [and] in conformity with § 16-­‐32-­‐10,” which states that it “shall also be the duty of the president and a committee of the faculty, . . . to arrange courses of study conforming to all acts of Congress, and prescribe any qualifications for the admission of students and any rules of study, exercise, discipline, and government as the president and committee may deem proper.” For more than half a century, the committee of the faculty mentioned in this legislation has been understood to be the URI Faculty Senate.

PROPOSAL: THE HONORS INSTITUTE Organizational Change – Creation of Honors Institute and Addition to Chapter 3 The Honors Program proposes expanding its scope and consolidating its operations under a new aegis, the Honors Institute.
The new institute contains the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – entities that already fall ad hoc under the umbrella of “Honors.” The creation of the Honors Institute will require organizational change.
It will reside in Chapter 3 of the University Manual.
The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be responsible for its oversight and report to the Provost.
The Executive Director and Assistant Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall be the Director and Assistant Director of the Honors Program.
An Advisory Council will be appointed by the Executive Director of the Honors Institute to include faculty representatives from Colleges across the University, Honors student leadership, and major external stakeholders.

The Honors Institute will not figure in Chapter 8 under “Centers and Institutes” (8.90.10-8.90.40) since the Honors Institute, an academic institute, is not the type of institute that this section was intended to govern.
The Honors Program is only one entity housed under the umbrella structure of the Honors Institute.
University Manual language [8.60.10-8.65.12] remains unchanged, including: ● Program Direction and Development.
The Director of the Honors Program in collaboration with the Teaching, Advising, and Assessment Committee shall be responsible for overseeing the Honors Program (8.64.10) ● “The Teaching, Advisement and Assessment Committee shall conduct periodic evaluations of the Honors Program and its separate components” [8.64.12].
Rationale for the creation of an Honors Institute In its current form, “Honors” at URI is minimally competitive with Honors education at our peer flagship institutions.

First, Honors education at URI largely does not meet national best practices and standards in terms of curriculum. (The Honors Program directors will be submitting a redesigned curriculum to the Faculty Senate soon.) Second, and more important to this proposal: The “Honors” ecosystem – the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities – is minimally integrated into the larger University, which has resulted in a lack of visibility and support.
In their “External Review Report” in 2023, National Collegiate Honors Council reviewers recognized that a transformation into an honors college was not feasible due to financial constraints at URI.
To compete with honors colleges all around us, and to house a 21st-century Honors Program, they recommended establishing an Honors Institute that pulls together officially the Honors Program, the Honors Colloquium, and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities.
This highly visible and fully integrated entity would operate on par with the colleges and thus enhance operational efficiency.

The reviewers stated that the creation of a formal Honors Institute will “result in significant long-term returns to the University by raising its academic profile, by attracting a portion of the large number of high-achieving students who are available in the wider area but do not choose to attend URI, and by increasing the amount of annual giving to URI.” Further still, the external reviewers affirm that the success of an Honors Institute “could have ripple effects that launch the University of Rhode Island toward the highest tier of institutions in the Northeast.” Budget The Honors Institute will keep its existing budget infrastructure.
This includes a Fund 100 base budget and external Foundation funding.
The current internal funding is sufficient for the Institute’s operations.
In the shift to an IBB model, Honors will be classified as a central service; we anticipate no decrease in levels of funding to Honors operations.

University Manual language for Chapter 3 3.60.10 The Honors Institute contains the Honors Program (see 8.60.10 - 8.65.12) and the Office of National Fellowships and Academic Opportunities. 3.60.11 The Executive Director of the Honors Institute shall report to the Provost and Executive Vice President for Academic Affairs, and shall have primary responsibility for administering the policies and procedures of this administrative unit. 3.60.12 The Executive Director shall be a non-voting ex officio member of the Honors Program Curriculum and Advisory Committee. UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND FACULTY SENATE REPORT OF THE EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE September 2005 The Executive Committee met regularly during the summer 2005 and after consideration, the FSEC agreed to bring forward to the Faculty Senate recommendations for changes to the UNIVERSITY MANUAL regarding the establishment of a committee on the undergraduate initiative on the Providence Campus and the University.
Following are each of the recommendations with rationale.
I.PROVIDENCE CAMPUS UNDERGRADUATE INITIATIVE COMMITTEE.
Background The Faculty Senate approved the establishment of a committee to provide oversight for the new Providence Campus Undergraduate Initiative, which is scheduled to begin in Fall 2006. Recommendation The Executive Committee recommends approval of the following new sections of the UNIVERSITY MANUAL: 5.83.10 The Providence Campus Undergraduate Initiative Committee shall oversee undergraduate programs offered on the Providence Campus to students admitted under the provisions of section 8.88.10.
The committee shall provide advice and support to the Vice Provost for Urban Programs and the Vice Provost for Academic Affairs during the initial stage of the initiative.
After the establishment phase, the committee shall review the initiative every 4 years.
Specific degree programs will be reviewed every three years on a staggered basis in accordance with the University’s current review policies. 5.83.11 The committee shall be comprised of the following members: one faculty member appointed by each department which offers an

undergraduate program at the Providence Campus; three faculty members appointed by the Faculty Senate in consultation with the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs from departments that do not offer undergraduate programs; and a designee of each of the following: the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs, the Vice Provost for Urban Programs, the Dean of University College and Special Academic Programs and the Dean of Admissions.
Faculty members shall be appointed for three-year staggered terms.
One of the Faculty Senate’s appointees shall serve as chair. 5.83.12 The committee shall meet on a regular basis and report annually to the Faculty Senate through the Curricular Affairs Committee on the status of the overall Providence Campus initiative.
Recommendations shall be forwarded to the Provost and Vice President for Academic Affairs and the Faculty Senate Curricular Affairs Committee for appropriate action.
II.AMENDING THE UNIVERSITY CALENDAR Background On May 9, 2005, the Faculty Senate approved a revised calendar for academic years through 2010.

Early in the summer it came to the Faculty Senate Executive Committee’s attention that the change in the official date of spring break for 2006 in the approved calendar for 2005-06 created serious confusion and uncertainty for members of the university community.
The change was from the traditional week (March 13-19, 2006), which had been published and promulgated previously, to the following week - March 20-26, 2006.
As people learned of this change in spring break scheduling, a number of problems were identified.
These problems especially affect those members of the campus who must make plans, schedules, travel arrangements, etc., at least one year in advance.
In order to avoid further confusion, the Executive Committee took the unprecedented step of acting for the Senate in accordance with section 4.3 of the Faculty Senate By-Laws and changing the spring semester calendar.
It was agreed that while such action was necessary at that time, the problems that occurred with regard to a last-minute calendar change should not happen again.
As a result, the Executive Committee proposes that, except for emergencies, it should not be possible to modify an approved calendar within 18 months of the start of the semester in question.

Recommendation The Executive Committee recommends approval of a clarification to section 8.70.13 (change is underlined) and the addition of a new section 8.70.14 as follows: 8.70.13 Recommendations regarding rescheduling class days missed within an academic year as the result of natural calamity, work stoppage, etc. shall be the responsibility of the Academic Standards and Calendar Committee, whose proposals will be subject to the approval of the Faculty Senate. 8.70.14 With the exception of circumstances stated in 8.70.13, changes to the calendar shall not be considered within eighteen months prior to the beginning of a semester.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE 224 PASTORE HALL, 51 LOWER COLLEGE ROAD, KINGSTON, RI 02881 USA, P: 401.874.2616 NOVEMBER 7, 2024 Dear Senators, Our community at-large and the faculty senate are both committed to protecting expressive speech as a core right underpinning academic freedom at the University of Rhode Island.
The recent DRAFT University of Rhode Island Board of Trustees Regulations Regarding Use of University Property, if approved without revision, would undermine this right.
It girds an overly vague set of conditions for the use of property with punitive consequences to be administered with vague guidelines and unfettered power.
Despite the inclusion of language which emphasizes learning, the letter makes no specific reference to academic freedom or its prominence in our University Manual (Chapter 6).
In this letter, I summarize the phases of the regulation's evolution over the past several months, as far as I am aware.
Then, I provide a short summary of the major concerns about the regulation that senators and other community members have identified.
Finally, I outline next steps.

Timeline • Spring/Summer 2024: Various communications from the URI administration indicated that lack of a policy pertaining to protest and its potential harms, particularly with respect to university property, was a concern. • Late August 2024: In writing, I requested senate review of policy drafts given potential bearing on academic life.
I received no reply in advance of the below steps. • Early October 2024: The DRAFT regulations were presented to the Administrative Policy Committee (on which I sit as Senate President) by Vice President of Administration and Finance (VPAF) Benson.
The DRAFT regulation was supplied one hour.
I raised concerns about austerity and potential impacts at the meeting, despite having to comment in real-time.
It was posted for public comment by the next day. • Mid-October 2024: Concerns arise in the community following communications to union members by the AAUP-URI executive director. • Late October 2024: Senate leadership meets with the VPAF and her staff.
The parties tentatively agree to participate in an ad hoc committee to assist with redress of the substantive problems, in addition to holding a forum at the next senate meeting.

Process issues about how these policies were shared and not properly vetted will be addressed at a future time.
Major Concerns Many senators have written to me by email or posted comments (400+) to the VPAFs policy site.
Of these, I am attaching four letters from senators and faculty, as well as a comment

written by the Rhode Island ACLU Executive Director and sent to the VPAF on the matter.
At a minimum, the following major areas of concern have been cited as areas of major concern around the proposed regulation. • The need for a policy or regulation to react to protest events on a campus that has essentially never seen violent protest, and which has a tradition of peaceful, participatory, and deliberative discourse, is ostensibly undocumented. • The policy is very vague on how response to property damage events will be pursued.
References to other handbooks, manuals, contracts, and laws seem to have been sufficient to manage any event involving damage to property in the past.

It is not clear how these policies will be enacted differently under this regulation, or if they should be. • Even if the regulation is stood up, there is a seemingly draconian presentation of severe punishments bereft of clear attendant policy, due process, and collective participation of appropriate university bodies. • There is a clear lack of common sense considerations in the regulation, such as faculty not being able to access their labs in off-hours, punishments for simple infractions such as littering with a flyer, and so on. • The forceful, top-down style, in the document and in procedural choices, contrasts starkly with the norms of a community that prides itself on academic freedom, constructive expressive speech, and civility, and with the expectations of a senate that is an equal partner in shared governance.
Charge to Attend and Engage Modern universities should form an intellectually safe, free marketplace of ideas.
Our faculty and students need to be able to express themselves without the weight of oppressive and potentially life altering consequences hanging over their heads while engaging in study, life and work.

This is especially true for our students who are learning to use their voices for change and good.
This DRAFT regulation is clearly not in-line with these imperatives.
Our task is to ensure that these issues are addressed through our deliberations and advocacy, and, if necessary, through legislation.
Please join us at the next Faculty Senate meeting on November 14 at 3:00 PM in the Hope Room, Higgins Welcome Center, at which time this matter will be discussed.
There are other important topics on the agenda, and many people will wish to speak on this matter, so please come prepared with concise statements.
We will not be addressing matters of university and senate process around policies and regulations at this meeting; however, we will be considering this need at another time.
Sincerely, Theodore (Ted) Walls URI Faculty Senate President, 2024-2025

Senator Koray Ozpolat 10/15/2024 Comments on the proposed regulations regarding the use of university property In principle, I agree that the university may establish reasonable standards and limitations regarding time, place and manner of use for university property.
Most of the listed limitations and prohibited activities (2a-2o) look reasonable.
However, I have three concerns (i) 2g. signs, posting and banners (ii) 3.
Enforcements and Violations, (iii) the timing of this proposal Motivation “Academic institutions exist for the transmission of knowledge, the pursuit of truth, the development of students, and the general well-being of society.
Free inquiry and free expression are indispensable to the attainment of these goals. “(AAUP Joint Statement) I believe it is important that URI remains an open space for students, faculty, and staff to exchange ideas and express themselves.
While protecting the university property matters, our strategic goal is to develop young minds to think critically and globally.

That’s how we can develop the leaders of the future who will “commit to addressing the most pressing issues facing our state and the global community” as mentioned in URI’s Strategic Priority-1 Concerns I am worried that with “somewhat” restrictive property policies and harsh sanctions for violations, the proposed regulations may broadly discourage students and faculty from engaging in campus activism, protests and demonstrations.
For example, if a student affixes a poster or a sign to the exterior of a building, could s/he face disciplinary action up to termination?
I would say “let them post” and URI employees can pull unauthorized posters later.
Why punish our students?
I am concerned about the timing of this proposal too.
What events put this proposal forward?
To the best of my knowledge, we did not have any encampments, or damage to campus property this year.
Is our administration under pressure from donors or politicians?
Conclusion After 13 years at URI, it is clear to me that political violence or destruction of campus property are not big issues in Kingston but on the contrary, it is lack of dissent and weak activism that slows down the growth of our students.

Many URI students have no idea or don’t care about what is going on beyond their small worlds!
Any policy that directly/indirectly discourages (the already weak) campus activism and demonstrations actually hurts the development of our students and I propose that • 2g is removed • The disciplinary actions for other violations be clarified • URI Administration shares with us - why now, justify the need for these restrictions • The introduction paragraph of the document can be extended to underline freedom of speech & assembly as vital elements of academic freedom and that buildings partially serve this purpose.

Thoughts on draft regulations for use of URI property: The draft is very legalistic and very top-down; it is “command-and-control” in tone.
The subtext of the regulations is that misbehavior will not be tolerated.
I’m not sure that is an eCective message to control the members of a University community.
The Introduction does not mention the special role of the University as a place where dissent is protected, and where the interruption of normal activities by peaceful civil disobedience is accepted for its potential contribution to civic discourse and social change.
As a place that honors free speech, the University should project collegiality and respect, even in laying down rules.
Some prohibitions in the draft are unnecessarily granular, treating such things as discarded leaﬂets (litter), impeding traCic, hanging banners, etc., which might occur during demonstrations, as punishable oCences.
History shows that prohibition of minor and incidental acts is often an invitation to law-breaking and/or an excuse to arrest, rather than an eCective way of controlling behavior.

It should also be noted that such prohibitions foster cynicism and undermine the trust of community members in their leaders and their pride in representing the institution.
The option of achieving community peace through consultation and dialogue with parties in conﬂict is not mentioned.
However, this is a far more eCective way to achieve the apparent goals of the draft, without threats and without talking down to the University community.
I recommend that: (1) this draft be revised in a negotiation process involving several sectors of the University community (administrators, staC, faculty, student organizations).
The revision should seek a balance between the administration’s control needs and recognition of the University’s special role in society as a place where dissent is protected; (2) minor, symbolic, and incidental acts be removed from the list of chargeable oCences; and (3) exceptions to the rules laid down be granted either in writing or verbally.
